title: Scalable, Programmable and Dense: The HammerBlade Open-Source RISC-V Manycore
problem: Conventional tiled manycore architectures struggle to simultaneously achieve scalability, programmability, and density as core counts approach 100K, forcing designers to sacrifice programmability for density or scalability for programmability.
motivation: General-purpose parallel processors that convert abundant silicon resources into high-density, programmable systems are essential for efficient computing at extreme scale.
method: HammerBlade is a system with thousands of processor cores arranged in a grid, built using RISC-V (an open instruction set that defines how processors execute commands). The design was validated with a real chip—a 2,048-core version manufactured using 14/16nm process technology, which shrinks transistors to fit thousands of cores on a single chip. Researchers tested it against various workloads to measure performance across different types of computation and data movement.
key_novelty: A grid-arranged processor that simultaneously achieves three competing goals—scalability to many cores, programmability, and density—without forcing engineers to sacrifice any one for the others.
contributions: Open-source RISC-V manycore architecture design achieving scalability, programmability, and density
Silicon-validated 2048-core ASIC implementation demonstrating practical feasibility at 14/16nm
Comprehensive benchmark evaluation methodology for diverse parallel workloads
